text:
The row can hold facts of its own, too, like a grade. Not on students, though: Ada got a B in Math and a C in History. Not on courses either: Math gave Ada a B, and Grace a C. It belongs to Ada in Math, on the pairing's own row. The next shape splits one thing in two.

Say a users table starts collecting profile details, like a display name and a bio. Lots of users, like Linus, never fill them in. So the profile moves to its own table. Each user has zero or one profile, and each profile belongs to exactly one user. The foreign key goes on the profile, the side that can't exist alone.

But a foreign key alone won't keep it to one. It'll happily take a second profile for Ada. Make that user ID unique, and the second one bounces. That's what makes it one to one. The last shape needs only one table.

An employee has a manager, and the manager's an employee too. So the foreign key points back into its own table. Ada's the CEO, with no manager. Grace reports to Ada, and Mina reports to Grace. Each row stores only its own manager, and the chain runs as deep as it needs: five levels here, down to an intern.

To read it, join the table to itself, as employee and as manager. A left join keeps Ada, with no manager. But a foreign key only checks that the manager exists. So what if Ada manages... Ada? Postgres takes it. One row updated. Keys guard the links between tables. To guard what goes in them, you need constraints.
